chapter_theme: The eighth ten, Arisil Kizhar's songs for Perunjeral Irumporai: foes who stirred the hive and paid tribute, the doom-fire for those who resolve without thought, a king beyond comparison whom praise cannot make credible, a learned sacrificer who sends his old counsellor to tapas, an army too large to count, a virali sent to the hill of the destroyer of Tagadur, a couch made of a beaten king's tusks; the preface names Adhiyaman and the razing of Tagadur.

71.reading: The poet tells Perunjeral Irumporai that those who provoked him suffered like small children who poked a rich hive where fierce bees sleep clustered like paddy heaped by the measure on the threshing floor: their towns burned, war smoke hid the quarters, their cattle with bulls and calves were driven off by his young archers, the herders' chief Kazhuvul bowed his head as churning ropes stood still at dawn, the people left for other lands to live as guests, and they brought him a great spot-browed elephant and rare jewels, praising him as a dread god, so that he takes tribute and leaves like a spirit that takes its offering and goes; had he not weighed the strong and the simple and shown grace, no one here would live.
71.nuance: The opening simile is double: the bees cluster like heaped grain, and the enemies are the children who stirred the hive, so their ruin is told as the sting of provoked bees, not as the king's first move. The still churning ropes at dawn (line 16) measure the cattle raid by the silence of the herders' homes. The poem ends on grace, but a grace that comes after the burning and the tribute.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem tells the burning of enemy towns, the seizing of cattle and the taking of tribute

comparisons.tenor: fierce bees clustered in the hive
those who provoked the king and suffered
the king who takes tribute and departs

72.reading: The poet tells the angry lord that those who provoke him, from the greatness of their enmity, do not fear taking up arms, resolve without deliberating and will not accept watchfulness, and in their folly do not know his nature, which is like that of the wise who served the first lords of his line, guarded the people and joined strength to knowledge; to them he is like the doom-fire of the world's end with its red flame and leaping sparks, as when at the evening that brings sleep a raging flood with strong waves overruns the earth and darkness spreads over the boundless quarters.
72.nuance: The poem sets two kinds of knowing against each other: the wise who know what is good (நன்றறி உள்ளத்துச் சான்றோர்) and the foes who do not know the king's nature from folly (மடம்பெருமையின்). The deluge and the doom-fire are both images of the world's end, so the king's anger is cosmic rather than personal.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's wrath against those who provoke him

comparisons.tenor: the king's deed against his foes
the king to those who provoke him

73.reading: The poet hails the one great king who is the measure of comparison for others while no other can be his, whether the strong or the simple reckon it, lord of Pukar on the Kaveri where women who drive herons from the marutham fields dance the kuravai day and night without taking off their jewels, shield of the Puzhiyar, lord of Kolli where bamboo grows and clouds creep, Poraiya of the bannered chariot, and says that though he has gone for many days to tell people that the king's wealth, manliness and giving exceed human measure, they do not believe him, and wondering whether they will believe it if the wise say so, he sees their minds bewildered and grieves at how to tell it.
73.nuance: The praise turns on the failure of praise: the king is beyond comparison, so the poet's report sounds like exaggeration, and the poem ends in the poet's own distress (வருந்துவல் யானே). The Chera is hailed as lord of Pukar on the Kaveri, a Chola port, which the poem does not explain. Two lines are lost after line 3.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's wealth, manliness and giving as beyond comparison

74.reading: The poet tells the king that he heard the learned texts and performed sacrifices without breaking his vows, pleasing the high ones; that his queen, with long dark hair like rippled black sand, adorned with fine jewels made at Kodumanam, pearls from Panthar and a gem cut and set by a skilled smith, bore a distinguished son who completed his learning and is fit to rule, so that he has paid his debt to those of his line; yet the poet is not amazed by these, but by the king's vow that he told his grey-haired elder, who knew everything and guided him, that generosity, dignity, wealth, offspring, the divine and all else belong to those who have tapas, and sent him to the wide forest.
74.nuance: The poem lists the goods a king is praised for (learning, sacrifice, a fine queen, a worthy son) only to set them aside (அன்னவை மருண்டனென் அல்லேன்): what amazes is the king's release of his old counsellor to austerity. The long middle passage on the making of a gem (lines 7 to 16) is the most obscure stretch of the decade.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's learning, sacrifice, family and his vow

75.reading: The poet tells Poraiya of the gold-garlanded elephants and well-running chariots that he is like the strong striped beast that kills the great tiger and slays the big tusker, and that if kings, Velir and others do not bow and follow him, their seats rich in paddy and in the sweet juice of milled sugarcane, open to all who come, will be reduced to hard ground where labourers tend dry plots of white millet and horse gram and do not know red paddy rice, so where would they have their lands famed in song to sport in together.
75.nuance: The threat is told through food: the rice and cane of the submissive lands against the millet and horse gram of the ruined ones. The middle lines (8 to 11) are hard to parse, and the contrast of fertile and barren land is the reading taken here.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's might with a warning to those who will not submit

comparisons.vehicle: இரும்புலி கொன்று பெரும்களி(று) அடூஉம் அரும்பொறி வயமான்

76.reading: The poet tells the lord of a land of wide fields that after the great battle with elephants, where he raised his spear, killed sword-flashing kings in their crowded ranks and crossed hard fords while the drum was struck, he healed his wounded men and ended the hard pain of his great host, as merchants who have crossed the sea refit their ship, and gave so that askers might live, never ceasing to give; the poet has come to see that faultless court, in a land where, when the clouds pour cool rain, the few ploughmen of many-seeded fields, wearing garlands of pakanrai from the cold ford white as washed cloth, find bright gems in their furrows.
76.nuance: The merchant simile makes the care of the wounded army a refitting after a voyage: the king's war is an enterprise, and its wounds a cost to be made good. The ploughmen who turn up gems with the soil give the land's wealth as something that rises unasked.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's care for his army, his giving and his rich land

comparisons.vehicle: பெரும்கடல் நீந்திய மரம்வலி உறுக்கும் பண்ணிய விலைஞர்
comparisons.tenor: the king healing his wounded army

77.reading: To travellers who ask how large an army the angry Poraiyan has, the poet answers that after the people fled and kings fell on the field and his men danced the victory thunangai, his chariots whose wheels rolled over corpses, his horses and his men were beyond counting and he could not count them, and that he sees in his army many elephants that refuse the tethering post, snap their stakes and sweep with their shadow the kites wheeling over the ground, spreading like the cattle of the Kongar of wet spears over the gravel upland.
77.nuance: The poem is an answer to a question, and its answer is that the army cannot be counted: the poet counts only the elephants, and those through a simile of spreading herds. The colophon calls it the clamour of a siege (உழிஞை அரவம்), but no fort is named in the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem measures the size of the king's moving army

78.reading: The poet tells a virali with a few bangles that if she goes on, the hill yonder, where a lovely white waterfall drops shining with a sound like the victorious drum, is the hill of the king who, in a land of many yields and forests where soft women cutting lotus with neythal call out in every grove to drive off parrots, razed Tagadur of bow-thick thickets guarded by valiant men, cut down the fierce enmity of those who glared at him and destroyed their hot front, and then had in his own land horses spread like goats and elephants spread like cattle.
78.nuance: The guide poem points the dancer not to the king's town but to his hill, recognised by its waterfall that sounds like his war drum, so the landscape itself announces him. The herds of horses and elephants at the end are the spoils of Tagadur, which the virali can expect a share of.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet directs a virali to the king's hill, a guide poem of praise

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the white waterfall

79.reading: The poet tells the king that he does not spare his life in battle and does spare nothing in giving among suppliants, honours the great and cherishes the small, that his fame has gone out from him whose shining tongue never knew desire for others' goods even in dream, whose manliness wore down his foes and whose chest bears a garland crushed by women's bangled arms, so that he is beyond measure; and therefore the victorious kings who would not come with him but stayed in their lands lost their elephants and bows, their drums were split and their royal elephant's tusks cut and made into a dread couch on which he sits, and he prays that the king's fame may stand unfailing like the hill of Ayirai, whose fearful god accepts no offering but the blood that spills from bodies shaken in battle.
79.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are built on one verb, போற்றலையே: the king does not guard his life but guards his giving. The couch made from the tusks of a defeated king's royal elephant turns the enemy's emblem into the victor's seat. The closing simile ties the king's fame to a war god who takes only blood.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving, courage and fame with a blessing

comparisons.tenor: the king's fame that should stand unfailing

80.reading: The poet tells the king that since his warriors, with broad chests where the sandal has dried, bangled strong forearms, wounded mighty shoulders and anklets, who never step back and bear bright swords, stand before his foes and say 'pay tribute to him who has undertaken protection', while the drum of victory, taken from his enemies on the great mountain, roars like the monsoon cloud and those with bows in their right hands praise him, how could the banners of his enemies' tall chariots with horses swift as the rising wind ever show at his border, he of unfailing firmness whose good fame is fixed on the earth.
80.nuance: The demand for tribute is put in the warriors' mouths as a protection offered (புரவு எதிர்ந்தோற்கு): tribute is the price of the king's guard. The enemy banner never even appears at the frontier, so the war is won before it is fought.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's warriors confront the foes at the front and demand tribute

comparisons.tenor: the swift horses of the enemies' chariots

patikam:8.reading: The decade's preface says that Perunjeral Irumporai, son of Kadungo of unfailing wealth by Padumandevi, daughter of Padumam, lord of the Velavi line, defeated together Adhiyaman of the many-speared army of the watery Kolli district and the two great kings, took their drums, umbrellas and jewels, performed the sacrifice of the battlefield, cut down the strength of the enemy so that their faultless women wept, razed Tagadur and won its defending fort, and that Arisil Kizhar of truthful speech sang this ten.
patikam:8.nuance: The preface gives the one fact the songs only point to: that the razing of Tagadur, named in 78, was a war against Adhiyaman fought alongside two other kings. The weeping women of line 8 are the only sign of the defeated side in the whole decade.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's lineage and conquests

links.note: Purananuru 5 tells a Chera, lord of a forest land where elephants spread like cattle, to keep away from those who cast off grace and love and to guard the realm as one rears a child; Patitruppattu 71 shows the king burning towns and taking cattle and tribute, then says that had he not weighed the strong and the simple and shown grace (அருளாய் ஆயின்), no one here would live.
links.teaches: Purananuru 5 asks for grace as the standing temper of a ruler's guard, while Patitruppattu 71 finds it only after conquest, as the sparing of the defeated who pay tribute, so the two Chera poems show grace counselled as a principle of rule and praised as a victor's restraint.

links.note: Akananuru 135 likens the heroine's shaken heart to Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir attacked it together; Patitruppattu 71 has Kazhuvul, chief of those who live by cattle, bow his head (கழுவுள் தலைமடங்க) when the Chera's archers drove off the herds.
links.teaches: Kazhuvul is besieged by a coalition of Velir in one poem and humbled by the Chera in the other, which shows his herders' stronghold as a repeated prey of greater powers and explains why an akam poet could use it as a byword for a heart under assault.

links.note: 71 line 25 has the king weigh the strong and the simple (உரவரும் மடவரும் அறிவுதெரிந்(து) எண்ணி) before he shows grace; 73 line 1 has the strong and the simple reckon the king (உரவோர் எண்ணினும் மடவோர் எண்ணினும்) and find no one to compare him to.
links.teaches: The decade turns the same pair round: first the king judges the wise and the foolish to decide whom to spare, then the wise and the foolish judge him and find no measure, so judgement runs both ways between the king and those he rules.

links.note: Kural 467 says to think and then resolve, and that to think after resolving is a lapse; Patitruppattu 72 says the king's foes, from the greatness of their enmity and their folly, resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்), unlike the wise who know his nature, and meet him as the doom-fire.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the rule as prudence in any task, while the Chera poem applies it to war and shows its breach as ruin, setting the wise counsellors who know the king against the foes who resolve unthinking, so deliberation becomes the line between the king's servants and his victims.

links.note: Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the one who has no comparison; Patitruppattu 73 calls the Chera one to whom others are no comparison (நினக்குப் பிறர்உவமம் ஆகா) and ends with the poet grieving (வருந்துவல் யானே) that people will not believe his praise.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the incomparable one the end of anxiety for those who come to him, but the Chera poet shows the same attribute, given to a king, bringing anxiety to the one who praises, since what has no comparison cannot be made credible to hearers.

links.note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because whatever is wanted is gained as it is wanted; Patitruppattu 74 says the king told his grey-haired elder that generosity, dignity, wealth, offspring, the divine and everything belong to those who have tapas (தவம்உடை யோர்க்கென), and let him go to the wide forest.
links.teaches: The Kural states the promise of tapas as a reason to strive, while the Chera poem shows a king applying it to another, releasing his aged counsellor from court to the forest, so tapas appears as the last stage of a life of royal service and its grant as a king's virtue.

links.note: 77 likens the Chera's many elephants to the cattle of the Kongar spreading over the gravel upland (கொங்கர் ஆபரந் தன்ன); 78 likens the horses and elephants he had in his own land after razing Tagadur to spreading goats and cattle (ஆபரந் தன்ன யானையோன்).
links.teaches: The decade moves the herd simile from the enemy's ground to the king's: first the elephants spread like a hostile people's cattle in an army on the march, then like home herds after victory, so one image marks war-strength turning into the settled wealth of peace.

links.note: Kural 443 says that to cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of rare things; Patitruppattu 79 says the king honours the great and cherishes the small (பெரியோர்ப் பேணிச் சிறியோரை அளித்தி), between lines on not sparing his life in war and sparing nothing in giving.
links.teaches: The Kural singles out honouring the great as a ruler's hardest gain, while the Chera poem pairs it with care for the small and sets both beside courage and giving, so the maxim appears as one term of a balanced royal portrait rather than a rarity standing alone.

links.note: The preface praises Perunjeral Irumporai for defeating Adhiyaman and razing Tagadur (தகடூர் எறிந்து), sung by Arisil Kizhar; Purananuru 230, by the same Arisil Kizhar, whose colophon names its subject as Ezhini the Adhiyaman who fell fighting at Tagadur, says Death lost more than the grieving, hungry world when it took him. On the reading that both refer to that war, one counts Tagadur's fall a glory and the other a loss to the whole world.
links.teaches: Read together, they show one court poet singing both sides of one war, the victor's fame and the fallen chief's elegy, so praise and lament were offices a poet filled by occasion, and the Tagadur campaign survives as triumph and as ruin in the same voice.

new_concepts.gloss: tribute paid to a king by those who submit to him
new_concepts.label_source: the text names it: திறைகொண்டு பெயர்தி (71 line 24), இடுக திறையே (80 line 10)

source_issues: 71-80: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); eight thurais are paadaan forms, 77 is உழிஞை அரவம் and 78 விறலியாற்றுப்படை. The patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
79 and 80: the colophon thurais are written without spaces (செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு, வஞ்சித்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு); normalised in puram_thurai names.

71 and 77 are marked vanji here against paadaan and உழிஞை அரவம்: 71 tells the burning of towns, a cattle raid and tribute; 77 measures the army and names no fort, so the siege thurai has no support in the poem.
73: two lines of dots (lost text) after line 3, per the lacuna flag; the poem is marked as it stands.
72 line 15 தீயிஅ is probably a misprint for தீயின்; 72 line 13 அஞ்சாறு is hard to divide.
71 line 13 ஆர்எயல் is probably ஆர்எயில், and line 14 தாணஇப் looks corrupt; 77 line 2 எனறனிர் is probably என்றனிர்; 80 line 2 கணண்கொண்(டு) may be a misprint.
71 line 11 has a comma inside the line (மதில்வாய்த், தோன்றல்).
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags) in every poem, and at 71 lines 7 and 25, 78 line 4, 80 line 14; the repaired readings are plausible.
patikam:8 line 12 (பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
